summary: This document specifies the DOTS signal channel, a protocol for a client to signal the need for protection against Distributed Denial-of-Service attacks to a server that can mitigate the traffic. A companion document defines the DOTS data channel. It obsoletes RFC 8782.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network is being flooded, the people running it often cannot see the attack well enough to defend it themselves, but a provider upstream can filter traffic. This document defines the small conversation that lets the network ask for that filtering, over a connection that still works when the network is congested.

subtitle: How a network under attack asks a provider to filter the traffic aimed at it.

tldr.problem: During a Distributed Denial-of-Service attack, a network owner often cannot tell what is hitting it but still needs to ask a provider that can filter traffic, and the request must get through even when links are congested.
tldr.mechanism: A DOTS client sends CoAP requests over DTLS/UDP or TLS/TCP, on port 4646, to a DOTS server, carrying CBOR-encoded mitigation scopes, with heartbeats and status notifications keeping the channel alive and informative.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9132 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8782, keeping the same CBOR keys while adding a comprehension-optional key range, an error summary and a table of default values.

facts.label: Happy Eyeballs preference
facts.value: UDP over IPv6, UDP over IPv4, TCP over IPv6, TCP over IPv4

today: RFC 9132 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2021. It obsoletes RFC 8782 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the standard for the DOTS signal channel.

sections.title: What the Signal Channel Does
sections.content:
A Distributed Denial-of-Service attack is a distributed attempt to make machines or network resources unavailable to their intended users. In most cases, sufficient scale for an effective attack is achieved by compromising enough end hosts and using those infected hosts to perpetrate and amplify the attack. The victim can be an application server, a host, a router, a firewall, or an entire network.

Network applications have finite resources: CPU cycles, the number of processes or threads they can create, the maximum number of simultaneous connections they can handle, and the resources assigned to the control plane. A TCP SYN flood, for example, is a memory-exhausting attack, while an ACK flood is a CPU-exhausting attack. Attacks on the link are carried out by sending enough traffic that the link becomes congested, likely causing packet loss for legitimate traffic. Stateful firewalls can also be attacked by sending traffic that makes the firewall maintain an excessive number of states, which may jeopardize its operation; the firewall then runs out of memory and can no longer instantiate the states required to process legitimate flows.

In many cases it may not be possible for network administrators to determine the cause of an attack. They may instead just realize that certain resources seem to be under attack. This document defines a lightweight protocol that allows a DOTS client to request mitigation from one or more DOTS servers for protection against detected, suspected or anticipated attacks, enabling cooperation between DOTS agents for a highly automated network defense that is robust, reliable and secure.

In typical deployments the DOTS client belongs to a different administrative domain from the DOTS server. For example, the client is embedded in a firewall-protected service owned by a customer, while the server is owned by a different entity, typically a service provider, that provides DDoS mitigation services. The server may or may not be co-located with the mitigator. The client can communicate directly with a server or indirectly via a DOTS gateway, and a gateway is often embedded in the customer's own equipment so that the customer domain is not exposed to the wider network.

The document adheres to the DOTS architecture, satisfies the requirements for the signal channel protocol and the use cases, and is a companion to the DOTS data channel specification, which defines the configuration and bulk data exchange mechanism supporting the signal channel.
sections.plainLanguage: A flood attack works by making a server run out of memory or CPU, or by filling a link so that real traffic is dropped. The network being attacked usually cannot see the attack well enough to defend itself, but a provider further out can filter the traffic. This document is the conversation between them.

sections.title: The Layering and the Port
sections.content:
The DOTS signal channel is built on top of the Constrained Application Protocol, a lightweight protocol originally designed for constrained devices and networks. The features of CoAP, its expectation of packet loss, support for asynchronous non-confirmable messaging, congestion control, small message overhead limiting the need for fragmentation, use of minimal resources, and support for DTLS and TLS, make it a good candidate on which to build the DOTS signaling mechanism.

DOTS clients and servers behave as CoAP endpoints, with a client behaving as a CoAP client and a server as a CoAP server by default, though either may take the other role for specific operations such as heartbeats. The layering puts the DOTS signal channel on CoAP, CoAP on TLS or DTLS, that on TCP or UDP, and that on IP.

In some cases a client and server may have agreed to use a specific port number, by explicit configuration or dynamic discovery. Absent such agreement, the DOTS signal channel MUST run over port number 4646 for both UDP and TCP, so the server listens on 4646. To use a different port, clients and servers SHOULD support a configurable parameter for it. The default port of 5684 for DTLS and TLS CoAP is not used, to avoid the discovery of services and resources described in CoAP and to allow different behaviour where a DOTS gateway and an Internet of Things gateway are co-located. Using a default port number also simplifies deployment where no explicit IP address configuration is required, and anycast addresses may be used for DOTS servers to simplify client configuration.

The channel uses the coaps URI scheme for CoAP over UDP secured with DTLS and the coaps+tcp scheme for CoAP over TCP secured with TLS. The signal channel can be established between two agents before or during an attack, and it is initiated by the client. The client can then negotiate, configure and retrieve the session behaviour with its peer. Once established, the agents may periodically send heartbeats to keep the channel active. At any time the client may send a mitigation request over the active channel, and while mitigation is active the server periodically sends status messages with feedback. Mitigation remains active until the client explicitly terminates it or the lifetime expires, and the server may also rely on the loss of the channel to trigger mitigation for preconfigured requests.

Messages are serialized using Concise Binary Object Representation, a binary encoding scheme designed for small code and message size, and the payload content type is application/dots+cbor. A DOTS client is entitled to access only the resources it creates, and cannot retrieve data related to mitigation requests created by other clients of the same client domain. DOTS agents MUST support the GET, PUT and DELETE CoAP methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The channel is built on CoAP, a small protocol made for devices with little memory and unreliable links, which is why it still works when the network is congested. By default it runs on port 4646, and its messages are packed into small binary objects rather than text.

sections.title: The Operations and Their Addresses
sections.content:
The DOTS server MUST support the path prefix /.well-known/ and the registered name "dots". Each operation is denoted by a path suffix appended to that prefix, giving three operations: mitigation at /mitigate, session configuration at /config and heartbeat at /hb.

The mitigation request adds two path options. The cuid, the Client Unique Identifier, is a globally unique identifier meant to prevent collisions among DOTS clients, especially those from the same domain, and it MUST be generated by the client. Implementations SHOULD set it by hashing one of the following with SHA-256: the DER-encoded ASN.1 representation of the Subject Public Key Info of the client's X.509 certificate, its raw public key, the pre-shared key identity it uses in the TLS 1.2 ClientKeyExchange message, or the identity it uses in the pre_shared_key TLS 1.3 extension. The hash output is truncated to 16 bytes by stripping off the final 16 bytes, base64url encoded with the two trailing equals signs removed, and used as the cuid. The cuid is intended to be stable when talking to a given server, and SHOULD NOT change over time, and it SHOULD be 22 characters to avoid fragmentation over UDP. If a client has to change its cuid, it MUST NOT do so while mitigations are still active for the old one, and it must delete and reinstall any aliases and filtering entries bound to the old cuid. A server MUST return a 4.09 Conflict error when the cuid is already in use by another client, and the peer MUST then generate a new one.

The mid is the mitigation identifier, which distinguishes one mitigation request from another within the same client domain, and the order of the path options matters, with 'mid' following 'cuid'.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request names the operation in its web-style address, and a mitigation request carries two identifiers: one for the client and one for the particular request. The client identifier is derived from the client's own key so that two clients in the same organisation cannot collide.

sections.title: Connecting to the Server
sections.content:
DOTS agents have to support both connectionless and connection-oriented protocols, so the signal channel is designed to operate with DTLS over UDP and TLS over TCP. A client may acquire a list of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, each of which can be used to contact the server over UDP and TCP. If no list is configured or discovered, the client adds the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses of its default router to the candidate list.

The procedure for choosing an address family and transport protocol exists to avoid long connection delays. If an IPv4 path works but the server's IPv6 path does not, a dual-stack client may experience a significant delay compared with an IPv4-only client in the same conditions. And if a middlebox blocks UDP, the client fails to establish a DTLS association and has to fall back to TLS over TCP, again with a significant delay.

To overcome these problems the client attempts to connect using both IPv6 and IPv4, and tries both DTLS over UDP and TLS over TCP, following a DOTS Happy Eyeballs approach similar to the mechanism defined in RFC 8305. The order of preference, most preferred first, is UDP over IPv6, UDP over IPv4, TCP over IPv6 and finally TCP over IPv4. This follows the address preference order of RFC 6724 and promotes UDP over TCP, to avoid TCP's head-of-line blocking.

After a connection is established the client MUST cache the outcome of each attempt for a specific time period to avoid thrashing the network, and the cache is flushed when its age exceeds a period on the order of a few minutes, for example 10 minutes. If the session is established with TLS because DTLS failed, the client periodically repeats the procedure to discover whether DTLS has become available, so that it can migrate the channel from TCP to UDP; such probing SHOULD NOT be done more often than every 24 hours and MUST NOT be done more often than every 5 minutes. When connection attempts are made during an attack, the client SHOULD use a connection attempt delay of 100 ms.
sections.plainLanguage: The client tries several ways of reaching the server in parallel, preferring the quickest and the least likely to be blocked, and remembers what worked so that it does not repeat failed attempts every time it needs to send something.

sections.title: Requesting Mitigation
sections.content:
Three methods are used by a DOTS client to request, retrieve or withdraw the status of mitigation requests. PUT is used to request mitigation, and during active mitigation PUT may carry mitigation efficacy updates. GET is used to retrieve the list of mitigations the server maintains, or to receive asynchronous status messages. DELETE is used to withdraw a request for mitigation. Mitigation request and response messages are marked as non-confirmable messages, and DOTS agents MUST NOT send more than one UDP datagram per round-trip time to the peer on average. A non-confirmable request is sent at regular intervals until a response is received; a client that cannot maintain a round-trip estimate MUST NOT send more than one such request every 3 seconds and SHOULD use an even less aggressive rate where possible. Mitigation requests MUST NOT be delayed because of probing-rate checks.

To request mitigation, the client uses the PUT method to send a mitigation request to its server. If the client is entitled to solicit the service, the server enables mitigation on its behalf by communicating the request to a mitigator, which may be co-located with the server, and relays the feedback of the selected mitigator back to the client.

The server couples the signal and data channel sessions using the client identity and optionally the 'cdid' value, so that it can validate whether the aliases in the mitigation request were really created by the same client over the data channel; if they were not, it MUST return 4.00 Bad Request. It uses the 'mid' and 'cuid' values to detect duplicate mitigation requests, and appends the parameter values associated with an alias name to the corresponding target parameters.

The result is reported with CoAP response codes: 2.xx for success, 4.xx for invalid requests and 5.xx when the server is in an error state or cannot currently provide mitigation. A request missing a mandatory attribute, without 'cuid' or 'mid', with multiple 'scope' parameters, or with invalid or unknown parameters, MUST be answered with 4.00. A request with a lifetime of 0 MUST be answered with 4.00. If the server does not find the 'mid' value in its configuration data it MAY still accept the request with a 2.01 Created response and try to mitigate the attack, and it MAY reject requests when it is near capacity or needs to rate-limit a particular client. When two mitigation requests of the same trigger type have overlapping scopes, the one with the highest numeric 'mid' value overrides the other.
sections.plainLanguage: To ask for filtering, the client sends a PUT naming the address ranges it wants protected. The server checks that the request is one it is entitled to make, passes it to the equipment that does the filtering, and answers with a status code. The client can later ask what is being filtered, update the result, or withdraw the request.

sections.title: Keeping the Channel Alive
sections.content:
To give an indication of signal health and to distinguish an idle channel from a disconnected or defunct session, a DOTS agent sends a heartbeat over the channel to maintain its half of it, and similarly expects a heartbeat from its peer, so that it may consider a session terminated after a prolonged absence of one. While the communication between the agents is otherwise quiescent, the client probes the server to ensure it has maintained cryptographic state, and the server does the same in reverse. Such probes can also keep the bindings of firewalls and stateful translators alive, which reduces the frequency of establishing a new handshake when a signal needs to be conveyed.

The heartbeat uses a non-confirmable PUT request with an expected 2.04 Changed response, and it occurs between an agent and its immediate peer, so it MUST NOT be relayed by a DOTS gateway. The request MUST NOT carry a 'cuid', 'cdid' or 'mid' path option. The mandatory 'peer-hb-status' attribute is set to true or false to say whether the agent has been receiving heartbeats from its peer in the last twice the heartbeat-interval period, which lets a peer detect or confirm connectivity problems and react. If a client receives a 2.04 response for its own heartbeats but no server-initiated heartbeats, it sets 'peer-hb-status' to false in its next heartbeat, and the server then tries another strategy for sending heartbeats.

The session configuration is negotiated and retrieved over the /config operation, with configuration freshness notifications so that a client learns when the server's view of the configuration has changed, and a delete operation to remove a configuration. Together with the heartbeats, these operations keep the channel usable and its state agreed on both sides.
sections.plainLanguage: Even when nothing is being asked for, the two sides check in with each other. That shows the connection is still alive, keeps any firewall or translator state from being torn down, and tells the client whether the server has noticed that the client has gone quiet.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
Errors returned by a DOTS server fall into two categories: those associated with CoAP itself and those generated while validating the data the client provided. In general there may be an additional plain text diagnostic payload to help troubleshooting in the body of the response.

The common CoAP errors implemented by DOTS servers are 4.00 Bad Request, returned when the client has sent a request that violates the DOTS protocol; 4.01 Unauthorized, when the client is not authorized to access the server; 4.02 Bad Option, when one or more CoAP options are unknown or malformed; 4.04 Not Found, when the client is asking for a 'mid' or 'sid' that is not valid; 4.05 Method Not Allowed, when the client is requesting a resource by a method the server does not support; 4.08 Request Entity Incomplete, if one or more blocks of a block transfer request are missing; 4.09 Conflict, when the server detects that a request conflicts with a previous one, with a response body formatted as "application/dots+cbor" containing the conflict clause; 4.13 Request Entity Too Large, which may be returned during a block transfer request; 4.15 Unsupported Content-Format, when the content format is used but the request is not formatted as "application/dots+cbor"; 4.22 Unprocessable Entity, when one or more session configuration parameters are not valid; and 5.03 Service Unavailable, when the server is unable to handle the request, for example because it needs to redirect the client to an alternate server.
sections.plainLanguage: The server answers with a standard set of error codes: the request was wrong, the client is not allowed to make it, the resource does not exist, the format was not what the server expects, or the server cannot help right now. The codes are the same ones CoAP uses, so a client can handle them without special cases.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authenticated encryption MUST be used for data confidentiality and message integrity, and the interaction between DOTS agents requires DTLS or TLS with a cipher suite offering confidentiality protection, following the guidance for secure use of TLS and DTLS. If TCP is used, an attacker may be able to inject reset packets or bogus segments even where TLS authentication is used; because the application data is TLS protected this will not result in the application receiving bogus data, but it will be a denial of service on the connection. That attack can be countered by the TCP Authentication Option, which rejects injected packets before they reach the TLS layer.

If the cuid is guessable, a misbehaving client from within the same domain can use the cuid of another client to delete or alter active mitigations, provided its messages pass the server's security checks. A similar attack can be achieved by a compromised client that sniffs the TLS 1.2 handshake and uses the client certificate to identify the cuid used by another client. That attack is not possible if the cuid is generated with a version 4 UUID, since such identifiers are not a deterministic function of the client certificate, and it is not possible with TLS 1.3 because most of the handshake is encrypted and the certificate is not visible to eavesdroppers.

A compromised client can collude with an attacker to request mitigation for a target resource, obtain the mitigation efficacy from the server and pass it to the attacker, who may then change the attack strategy. This can be prevented by monitoring and auditing clients, and by authorizing a client to request mitigation only for specific target resources: an application server is authorized to request mitigation for its own addresses, while a mitigator can request it for any target resource in the network.

Rate-limiting requests, including those with new cuid values, from the same client defends against denial-of-service attacks that would otherwise vary the cuid to exhaust server resources, and such policies SHOULD be enforced on gateways and servers. To prevent leaking internal information outside a client's domain, gateways in the client domain SHOULD NOT reveal identification information about internal clients unless configured to do so. Servers MUST verify that requesting clients are entitled to trigger actions on a given IP prefix, and MUST NOT authorize actions beyond the client's own domain resources. Finally, gateways may lead to infinite forwarding loops, so the Hop-Limit Option is used to prevent and detect them.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole conversation is encrypted, and the client identifies itself with an identifier derived from its own key so that a compromised client in the same organisation cannot pretend to be another one and cancel its protection. A server only lets a client ask for filtering on addresses that belong to that client.

items.desc: One or more session configuration parameters are not valid.

items.label: Service Unavailable
items.desc: The server cannot handle the request, for example because it must redirect the client.
